Do any of you remember Digg, and do you think this trend of sites growing large and then forsaking their users for money is just a one off thing or a pattern.

You almost can't avoid it.

Look, having a great deal of traffic has a downside. It costs money to run. So you need an influx of capital. That requires someone willing to make an investment. You run around fine afterwards, and everyone is happy. Problem is that the investor can't just give you free money. They need a return on their investment...and the only way to do that is to monetize. When that happens, sites often lose the things that made them great in the first place.

And, yes. It'll happen to Voat as well..although hopefully not before it stands as a place for ideas for at least a decade.
That isn't a bad idea, and it might work, since alot of ex-redditors would support us.
We could also get the folks over at /v/politics to figure out a tyranny-free management system, like with rotating admins.

And, in ten years, when the honeymoon is over?

Somewhat related. Snoop shouldn't have given 50m to reddit. That's not an opportunity; it's an obligation. Sites like reddit and voat are low yield investments. You can expect every tnbt to have a 5 or 10 year roi.

Isn't that essentially what Reddit Gold is? However, from my understanding, the revenue generated from Gold isn't enough to sustain Reddit as a whole. It might work for a smaller site like Voat, but once it gets too large, you need to monetize in different ways.
Reddit never really tried advertising. Would that model work?

Yeah, while maybe just maybe it can be avoided with a transparent non-profit foundation, it's unlikely. Just the cycle of business for a site to forget to cater to it's userbase- look at AOL, Facebook. It's social entropy. But that social entropy serves a greater capitalist purpose of promoting atomism and therefore maximized consumption. Our forums are transitive, and accordingly, our relations, our social selves. It's not just that our infometrics have been monetized, but, in many ways, through this process, our very social structure is debased.

So with time, Voat also will go astray, become greed-based, and alienate it's users as the power hierarchy yields over to another cabal of San Jose codebros with MBAs. That's not a bug, you must understand. That's a feature.

It was community based before it turned into a constant ad stream and now I'm lost in an ocean of paid content which is incredibly frustrating. Unfortunately I feel like a product pretty much everywhere I go online these days and I find that horrendously discomforting. I've just been reading some introductions to voat and I love the attitude so far. It's wonderfully welcoming and I really enjoy how much the users encourage common courtesy... so yeah, it's definitely a pattern!

Sadly yeah. Large websites have large running costs so need a larger income. What's interesting about Reddit specifically is that the users know this and are happy to help (just look at Reddit Gold).

Maybe if websites ran polls or something and allowed users to vote on the different ideas, and therefore participate in the monetization process, that would make things easier. That way the users would be onside before new features were even implemented.

This will be true of all websites. However, there a few p2p solutions in the works, and hopefully a decentralized community will be able to avoid not only monetization, but also be free from those who seek to impose control across the whole community.
